director.chapterArc: Rainbound calculation becomes deliberate labor; the blade’s activation opens a tactile Kindling memory that moves from sacrifice and communal belonging through public embarrassment to familial validation of usefulness over beauty. The falling spruce snaps Jab back into the present, where a failing carrying frame narrows his options. The chapter then pivots from material scarcity to emotional triage: Jab repeats the unbearable truth about their parents, replaces reassurance with a concrete promise, and carries Tonk into a colder, harder night.
director.restraintNote: Keep Original Calder grounded in Jab’s bodily arithmetic: wet, cold, load, materials, remaining days. The memory should feel physically triggered rather than nostalgically narrated. Let humor stay dry and familial, awe remain matter-of-fact, and grief register through small failures of composure rather than vocal weight. Tonk’s fever speech is thin and intimate, never performed as theatrical delirium. After every colored passage, restore the base narrator completely.

cues.delivery: Land the solitude as a dry practical defect; no self-pity, only the faint absurdity of having no one available to object.
cues.from: Nobody argued with him, which was the whole trouble with being the only one there.
cues.through: Nobody argued with him, which was the whole trouble with being the only one there.
cues.reason: A brief wry release establishes Jab’s isolated decision-making.

cues.delivery: Use affectionate communal dryness: the ceremony matters precisely because nobody treats it as pageantry. Keep every joke tossed away.
cues.from: That was the whole rule of the thing. The families had built the ceremony themselves in his father's aunt's own lifetime, when the children first started waking and nobody had any idea what to do with their hands, and they had put it at the end of the run for a reason his father's aunt gave to every child who asked: we're not going to stand in the river asking the river for anything while we still want fish out of it. Which was a joke. Which was also, like most of what she said, not entirely a joke.
cues.through: So the Kindlings happened in the last week of the smoking, when everyone was tired and everyone smelled like alder smoke and the racks were black with split fish to the far end of the bar, and the whole business had the feel of a thing tacked onto the end of a good season rather than a solemn occasion arranged in advance. Jab had always liked that about it. Nobody had cleaned up. Nobody was wearing anything special. His cousin had a fish scale stuck to her cheekbone through the entire thing and did not know, and four people saw it and none of them told her, and that was his people entirely.
cues.reason: The ritual’s improvised humor defines Jab’s people and prevents ceremonial grandeur.

cues.delivery: Let the loss register only in the unexpected bodily lurch; do not sentimentalize the hook or announce its symbolism.
cues.from: It went. He did not see it go. There was no moment where it was visible and then was not; there was only a hook in his fingers and then cold water running through empty fingers, and a small unreasonable lurch under his ribs that he had not been prepared for at all.
cues.through: It went. He did not see it go. There was no moment where it was visible and then was not; there was only a hook in his fingers and then cold water running through empty fingers, and a small unreasonable lurch under his ribs that he had not been prepared for at all.
cues.reason: Giving away the handmade object is the memory’s first genuine emotional cost.

cues.delivery: Break the answer naturally through chattering teeth; the laugh comes from timing and adolescent honesty, never from playing for it.
cues.from: "I have not," Jab called from the water, and that got a bigger laugh than it deserved, and his teeth were chattering by then so it came out in pieces.
cues.through: "I have not," Jab called from the water, and that got a bigger laugh than it deserved, and his teeth were chattering by then so it came out in pieces.
cues.reason: Jab’s interruption briefly punctures the ceremony’s pressure.

cues.delivery: Keep the unnamed man’s absence inside the hesitation around his name; deliver the testimony plainly, as something Jab can bear only because it is useful.
cues.from: "Mine," said a man from the far end, whose name Jab had gone six weeks now without being able to say aloud without stopping. "I taught him nothing. He carried wood for me for a winter when my back went and he never once said a word about it, and I want that counted."
cues.through: "Mine," said a man from the far end, whose name Jab had gone six weeks now without being able to say aloud without stopping. "I taught him nothing. He carried wood for me for a winter when my back went and he never once said a word about it, and I want that counted."
cues.reason: The remembered speaker carries a fresh, deliberately unspoken loss.

cues.delivery: Widen gently into recognition, not spectacle: Jab discovers that his competence was assembled by a whole community. Let the final understanding arrive quietly.
cues.from: It went on. Eleven people, in the end. He had not expected eleven. He had expected his parents and his aunt and perhaps the old man, and instead they kept starting up out of the crowd, and one of them was a woman he had only ever spoken to about her dog, and she said, mine, I taught him to swim, and he was a coward about it for one whole summer and then he was not, and Jab stood in the water with his face burning in the cold and understood, in a way that he had not understood at any point in thirteen years of living among them, how much of him had been put there on purpose by other people's hands.

cues.reason: This is the ceremony’s deepest revelation of belonging.

cues.delivery: Give the aunt’s contradiction absolute deadpan authority; she can invent a custom and still submit to it without noticing the joke.
cues.from: He came up out of the water onto the gravel with his legs gone, and the wind found him, and somebody's blanket came around his shoulders from behind and was taken away again immediately by his father's aunt, who said the boy needed to be cold for this next part, and then muttered that she did not know why, it was just how they'd always done it, which was a thing she said about a custom she had personally invented eighteen years earlier.
cues.through: He came up out of the water onto the gravel with his legs gone, and the wind found him, and somebody's blanket came around his shoulders from behind and was taken away again immediately by his father's aunt, who said the boy needed to be cold for this next part, and then muttered that she did not know why, it was just how they'd always done it, which was a thing she said about a custom she had personally invented eighteen years earlier.
cues.reason: Her dry inconsistency releases tension before the metal is presented.

cues.delivery: Treat the warmth as exact anatomy, then allow wonder only in the realization of unity. No mystical swell; discovery remains intimate and physical.
cues.from: And then the metal got warm.
cues.through: It was not large. That was the part he had never once been told and later told everyone — a warmth the size of a coin, low, under the breastbone and a finger's width behind it, in a place he had gone thirteen years without having any reason to notice. Then a second warmth started up in his hand, the right one, down in the meat of the palm. And then, with no gap between the two things at all, came the knowing: those were not two warmths. They had never been two. They were one warmth that had been in him the whole time, and the only new thing in the world was that they were now in the same room and could see each other.
cues.reason: Jab first recognizes the connection between his body and the inherited metal.

cues.delivery: Hold close to Jab’s mortification while the family identifies the obvious with merciless practicality. Keep the exchange clipped and unadorned.
cues.from: What Jab had was a fish knife.
cues.through: "It is a fish knife. I have used that knife. That is the knife."
cues.reason: The unimpressive fish-knife shape creates the chapter’s central comic reversal.

cues.delivery: Narrow into a thirteen-year-old’s contained dread of failing in public; articulate each gutter of light clearly and keep the panic entirely inside the final thought.
cues.from: He did not call it. Nothing about it was his idea. A line woke up along the working edge and ran outward from his hand, thin as a hair and the low amber color of a coal with ash on it — and two-thirds of the way along, at the fat part of the belly, it stuck. It guttered there. It went out and came back and went out, three times, at that one curve, while sixty people watched, and Jab's whole face went hot and he thought, with total clarity, it can't even do it properly.
cues.through: He did not call it. Nothing about it was his idea. It guttered there. cues.reason: The unstable light makes Jab believe his Kindling is defective before everyone watching.

cues.delivery: Warm only around Tonk’s reaching hand and laugh. The love is retrospective and precise—the one sound Jab preserved—not openly mournful.
cues.from: And from a carrying frame on his mother's back, where he had been asleep through the entire business, his brother woke up.
cues.through: That was the sound Jab remembered. Not the men, not his aunt, not the word somebody said. His brother laughing at his ugly blade across ten feet of gravel at dusk.
cues.reason: Tonk’s delighted response transforms Jab’s shame into the memory he values most.

cues.delivery: Make the father’s analysis practical enough to conceal its tenderness. The hand on Jab’s head is the only overt reassurance; do not underline it.
cues.from: "It's a working shape." His father set the wrist down. "You know what that belly's for? It's for when you can't get behind a thing and you have to cut it from the side. It's for wet wood. It's for a rope under tension, which will take a straight blade away from you and give it back in the water." He put his hand flat on the top of Jab's head, once, briefly. "Mine came out like a nail. It took me two years to make it into anything, and I'll tell you what I got for those two years: a blade that is very good at going into things and no good at all at coming out of them."

cues.reason: His father validates the blade by explaining its real usefulness.

cues.delivery: Keep the comparison blunt and fond, then make the invitation to eat an ordinary rescue from embarrassment.
cues.from: "Mine's prettier than yours," his father said. "Come and eat. You've gone a color."
cues.through: "Mine's prettier than yours," his father said. "Come and eat. You've gone a color."
cues.reason: The father closes the lesson with understated family humor.

cues.delivery: Give the mother’s verdict unhurried bluntness. It is permission to become himself, offered without softness or ceremony; let the last warning remain practical.
cues.from: And his mother, who had come up with Tonk still reaching over her shoulder, and who had not said anything at all yet, leaned in past him and looked at the blade for a long moment, and then said the only thing anybody said that night that Jab had kept whole and unworn for four years:
cues.through: "Well, it looks like you," she said. "That's the whole of it. You'll spend a while wishing it looked like somebody else. Don't spend too long."
cues.reason: Her words state the memory’s lasting lesson about identity and utility.

cues.delivery: Allow the sting in his eyes without assigning it a single cause. Rain gives him cover; keep the admission private and quickly contained.
cues.from: Jab stood in the rain with the light still running along his blade, a thin amber line in a gray wood, and his eyes were stinging and he let them, because there was nobody up here and the rain was doing most of the work anyway.
cues.through: Jab stood in the rain with the light still running along his blade, a thin amber line in a gray wood, and his eyes were stinging and he let them, because there was nobody up here and the rain was doing most of the work anyway.
cues.reason: The present absorbs the memory’s accumulated love and loss.

cues.delivery: Thin, fever-soft, and genuinely searching; Tonk asks as though the answer may still be ordinary.
cues.from: "Where's Mum gone?"
cues.through: "Where's Mum gone?"
cues.reason: The child’s question opens the final emotional crisis.

cues.delivery: State the deaths flatly because Jab has learned that clarity is the least harmful version. Let the repeated nature of the sentence—not vocal breaking—carry the trauma.
cues.from: "She died when the bridge went," Jab said. "In the water. Dad too. They're not coming, and I'm not going to tell you they are."
cues.through: "She died when the bridge went," Jab said. "In the water. Dad too. They're not coming, and I'm not going to tell you they are."
cues.reason: Jab must deliver the unbearable truth as functional care.

cues.delivery: Build safety from concrete inventory—fire, verses, thumb, stillness. Keep Jab steady rather than soothing; his promise is physical and enforceable.
cues.from: "I know." Jab got his arm under him and shifted him so that his head lay in the crook of it instead of on the hide, which was worth more than the bark some nights. "It's coming anyway. So here's what we're going to do. I've got a fire that'll go all night, and I've got the four verses, and when the big one comes you're going to hold onto my thumb as hard as you like and I'm not going to move."
cues.through: "I know." Jab got his arm under him and shifted him so that his head lay in the crook of it instead of on the hide, which was worth more than the bark some nights. "It's coming anyway. So here's what we're going to do. I've got a fire that'll go all night, and I've got the four verses, and when the big one comes you're going to hold onto my thumb as hard as you like and I'm not going to move."
cues.reason: Jab answers Tonk’s fear with a specific survival ritual.

cues.delivery: Make Tonk’s flatness more unsettling than tears: small, depleted, and intent on preserving the exact familiar detail.
cues.from: Tonk got a fist around Jab's thumb, and shut his eyes, and after a moment said, in a small flat voice with nothing childish in it:
cues.through: "You have to say the bit about the cousin."
cues.reason: His request for the cousin verse reveals lucid need inside the fever.

cues.delivery: Let the childish solution arrive with exhausted certainty. The humor is tender but must not dispel the danger around them.
cues.from: "Say it wrong, then," Tonk said.
cues.through: "Say it wrong, then," Tonk said.
cues.reason: Tonk accepts imperfection as long as Jab continues the ritual.
